title: mPDF 5.7.1 - image displays as a broken [x]

content: # mPDF 5.7.1 - image displays as a broken [x] When generating PDFs with mPDF version 5.7.1, encountering a placeholder `[x]` instead of an actual image is a frustrating but common hurdle. The issue arises because mPDF does not process external URLs for embedded images in the same way modern web browsers do. By default, the library expects image resources to be local files present on the server's filesystem. If you attempt to load an image via `src="https://www.google.pl/images/srpr/logo11w.png"`, mPDF will fail to fetch it, resulting in the broken icon. To resolve this, you must ensure the image file exists locally within a directory that mPDF can access. This is not merely a configuration setting; it is a fundamental architectural difference between rendering HTML in a browser versus generating a static PDF document. The library builds the document by reading and parsing source files relative to its working directory, not by making HTTP requests to external hosts during the generation process. The most effective solution involves copying the image file into your project's root or a dedicated assets folder. Once the file is local, you can reference it directly in your HTML string. For instance, if you place `logo11w.png` in the same directory where your PHP script resides, you can update your code to: ```php $html = ''; ``` This approach eliminates the dependency on external network calls and ensures that mPDF can locate the binary data required for rendering. You do not need to use `realpath()` or complex path manipulation unless your project structure is unusually deep, but keeping the reference relative and simple is often the cleanest strategy. If you are working within a Laravel application, the location of the image becomes even more critical. mPDF will look for images relative to the script's execution context. If your HTML string is constructed inside a controller or a view that loads from a specific blade template, the path resolution might differ. In such cases, placing the image in the public assets folder, such as `public/images/logo11w.png`, and adjusting the source to `src="images/logo11w.png"` is the standard practice. It is important to note that mPDF 5.7.1 does not support fetching remote images via HTTP headers or cURL requests internally. This limitation exists because PDF generation requires a deterministic, offline process once the script starts. All assets must be pre-loaded or available as static files on the disk before the rendering engine attempts to parse them. Some developers attempt to use base64 encoding to bypass this by embedding the image data directly into the HTML string. While technically feasible, this approach inflates memory usage and makes the generated PDF file significantly larger if the image is high resolution. For small icons or logos, local files remain the superior choice for performance and maintainability. If you are building a solution where external images are unavoidable, consider using an intermediate step to download and cache the remote asset before passing the HTML to mPDF. This decouples the PDF generation process from external network availability, ensuring your PDF output remains consistent regardless of internet connectivity at the moment of rendering. For those maintaining legacy systems or integrating with older PHP frameworks, understanding these constraints is vital. The transition from browser-based DOM parsing to PDF-specific rendering engines requires a shift in how resources are managed. If you find yourself needing more robust image handling capabilities, such as dynamic fetching or cloud storage integration, libraries like `dompdf` might offer different configuration options, though they also require careful handling of external resources.
